(c) As per the standard AIDS case definition adopted under the 
programme, all States/UTs are reporti ng AIDS cases on a monthly basis to 
National AIDS Control Organisation. However, as there is high under reporting 
of cases, we are relying on HIV surveillance mechanism as HIV is the first 
stage of disease. This enables us to tr ack the course of AIDS epidemic in the 
country. The National AIDS Control Organization conducts annual round of 
HIV sentinel surveillance in designated sites all over the country. The data thus 
collected is used to monitor HlV trends in various risk groups of population over 
time and in different geographical areas. This set of data is also used to work out 
estimated number of HIV infections in the c ountry on an annual basis. This 
process takes care of minimizing the participation bias by the individuals who 
might oe avoiding coming to Government Health Centres. Such bias is taken care 
by doing the surveillance activities using "unlinked anonymous" metnodology 
and consecutive sampling. This methodology has been recognized as a 
globally accepted methodology based on the guidelines issued from WHO and 
UNAIDS from time to time.

are given to NGOs through the State AI DS Control Societies for undertaking 
Targeted Interventions addressing mainly the groups at higher risk of contracting 
HIV infection and to provide care & support services for people living with

Disused Rail routes/lines in Tamil Nadu 
*86. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of railway routes/lines which are in disuse in Tamil Nadu; 
(b) the length of such routes with railway stations on the routes and the 
numbers of years of disuse of each route; 
(c) the reasons for disuse in each case; and 
(d) when the recent assessment of each route was done to consider 
operating trains on these routes? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) to (d) 
The details of rail routes/lines that are in disuse over Tamil Nadu are as under:- 
(1) Nidamangalam—Manargudi section having distance of 13 Kms was 
closed for traffic during 1976. Rajapayam, Chavadi Halt, 
Hariddhra, Nadhi Halt stations were on this route. 
(2) Peralam—Karaikal section having distance of 23.10 Kms was closed 
for traffic during 1987. Peralam, Ambegarattur, Tirunallur, 
Koraivovilpattu and Karaikal stations were on this route. 
(3) Mayiladuturai—Taragambadi section having distance of 29,35 Kms. 
was closed for traffic during 1987 Mayilduturai Town, 
Sembanarkoil, Akkur, Tirukadaiyur, Thillaiyadi, Poraiyar stations 
were on this route. 
(4) Agasthiyampalli—Kodikarai section having distance of 9 Kms was 
closed for traffic during 1987. There is no station on this section. 
In view of the heavy loss every year on these line, a work-study was 
conducted by Railways which recommende d for closure of these sections. 
The above sections were closed in th e respective years mentioned above and 
permanent way structure were also removed.

"Total Safety" in Railways 
*87. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently some fresh initiatives have been taken 
to achieve "total safety" on the Indian Railways; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof including  specific steps contemplated for 
addressing the problem of unmanned crossings and fresh guidelines laid down, 
if any, or machinery established to  enforce accountability for the railway 
accidents caused, especially, due to human failure? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) and (b) 
Safety is accorded the highest priority on Indian Railways and adoption of new 
measures to improve safety, reduce the number of consequential accidents and 
resulting fatalities is continuous process. 
A drive was recently launched on the Railways to observe a total safety 
fortnight and to streamline all aspects of  safety including maintenance of all 
assets, availability of essential spares and materials, operation of trains, human 
failures, inspections and to rectify defects noticed during the drive. The drive 
involved officers and supervisors of all departments for monitoring the aspects 
concerning their areas of working. 
Necessary action is taken against the staff found directly responsible for the 
accident or whose action may have led to circumstances 
38 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
responsible for the accident. The machinery to enforce accountability for railway 
accidents already exists on the Indian Railways. 
One of steps taken to improve the safety at unmanned level crossings is 
their progressive manning. Railway undertakes the manning of unmanned level 
crossings based on the criteria/guidelines laid down which includes volume of 
rail and road traffic moving through level crossing, plying of motor vehicles and 
visibility criteria. Apart from manning of unmanned level crossings steps are 
taken to improve basic infrastructure at level crossings, improving road 
surface, provision of speed breakers/rumble strips on approaches, availability 
of signboards and publicity to improve safety awareness among road users etc. 
Train drivers are instructed to whistle continuously while approaching level 
crossings.

Effect of Forest Conservation Act, 1980 on developmental works 
†*89.   SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Forest Conservation Act, 1980 is the main 
hurdle in implementation of Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana and other 
developmental work particularly in Orissa; 
(b) if so, the number of cases seeking permission for construction of 
roads on the forest land falling enroute and other development works under the 
scheme forwarded by the State Government during last three years alongwith 
the number of cases cleared and pending so far; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government for a permanent solution to the 
problem? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) to (c) No, Sir. Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, is a regulatory and not 
a prohibitory Act. It has the enabling provisions for the Central Government to 
grant permission for non-forestry use of forest land for developmental 
purposes. Proposals for forestry clearance for construction of roads under Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) are dealt 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi,   
41 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
on priority basis, in respect of all the States/Union Territories including the 
State of Orissa. Further, for up-gradation of roads constructed in forest areas 
prior to 1980, from 'Kutchcha to Pucca' , without widening , prior permission 
under this Act is not required. Guidelin es have already been issued by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forest on 30th April 2005 in this regard. 
However, if any such project falls in a National Park/ Sanctuary, prior 
permission of National Board of wildlife (NBWL) and the Supreme Court, is 
essential. In so far as other developmental works are concerned, Central 
Government has already granted general approval under this Act on 3rd January 
2005, for infrastructure development projects upto 1.0 hectares, to be 
implemented by Government Departments, like school, dispensary/hospital, 
electric lines, drinking water, rain water harvesting structure minor irrigation 
canal, non-conventional sources of energy, skill upgradation/vocational training 
centre, power sub-stations etc. 
During last three years (01-07-2002 to 01-07-2005), Government of 
Orissa has submitted a total of 106 development project proposals including 
12 for construction of roads (2 under PMGSY). Out of total proposals 
received, 75 projects including 11 for construction of roads (2 under PMGSY), 
have been approved by the Central Government on merit and ecological 
considerations. Only 5 cases of Orissa are under various stages of consideration 
of the Central Government. None of these case pertain to construction of roads. 
Remaining 26 cases have either been rejected for valid reasons, or returned to 
the State Government due to incomplete information. No proposal for 
construction of roads on forest lands in Orissa including construction under 
PMGSY, is pending with the Central Government.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) The Principal and Controlling Officer, 
Government Homoeopathy Medical College, Thiruvananthapuram,

Course in Homoeopathy 2000-2001 for information to the Secretary, Central

and by the CCH in their respective meetings held in February, 2001 and March,

Thiruvanathapuram vide Council's letter dated 9.5.2001 that if Government of 
Kerala wanted to conduct Nursing-cum-Pharmacist Course in Homoeopathy,

So far there is no statutory body to regulate any course relating to 
nursing or pharmacy in the Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy. 
The Central Pharmacy Council for Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy Bill,

Parliament for regulation of Pharmacy or

would be required so that infrastructural requirements for smooth conduct of 
graduation and post-graduation courses in Homoeopathy medicine are not 
compromised. 
The Nursing-cum-Pharmacist course does not require the approval of 
Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS). The CGHS have a post of

experience as a Homoeopathy Pharmacist in Government or recognized 
private Homoeopathic hospital/dispensar y or three years experience under a 
registered Homoeopathic practitioner.

Research on pest resistance of Bt. Cotton 
490. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, according to a study by  Central Institute for Cotton 
Research (CICR), a few years down the line, Bt. cotton might die a natural death at 
the hands of American bollworm, the pest it is supposed to resist; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the CICR has developed a model that 
predicts exactly how many years it would take the notorious pest to become 
completely resistant to Bt. cotton; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to arrest its impending 
decline? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) The study conducted by Central 
Institute for Cotton Research (CICR) showed that the American bollworm will 
develop resistance to Bt-cotton after a few years depending mainly 
52 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
on the extent of area under Bt-Cotton in the country. With the current rate of 
increase in the area under Bt -cotton, it is likely to take about 11-12 years for 
the pest to develop resistance to Bt -Cotton, if appropriate resistance 
management strategies are not properly implemented. However, with 
implementation of proper strategies as suggested by CICR, it is possible to delay 
resistance by at least 30-40 years, if not more. 
(b) Yes, a stochastic model 'Bt-Ad apt' was developed to simulate 
the rate of resistance development of H. armigera to Cry 1 Ac under Indian 
farming condition. Full details of the software and results of the prediction 
modelling study have been published in 'Current Science' in October 
2004. The model integrates genetic and ecological parameters of 
H. armigera in relation to its response to the Cry1 Ac expressing Bt cotton. 
The model can predict the time that would take for bollworm to develop 
resistance in different cotton-growing districts of the country, based on 
the input statistics of area under Bt-cotton in each of the districts, or even 
the proposed area to be cultivated under Bt-cotton. 
Simulation analysis showed that relative survival rate of the Cry1Ac 
resistant homozygous (RR), heterozygous (RS) and homozygous susceptible 
(SS) H. armigera genotypes on Bt-cotton, was the most important factor 
influencing resistance development. In the order of significance, the other 
factors that had the greatest impact on resistance development were, the 
relative proportion of area under Bt-cotton, dominance of the resistant allele 
and initial frequency of resistant alleles in field populations. The extent of 
population reduction in Bt-cotton and non-Bt crop due to pest control, was 
found to have a significant impact on the rate of resistance development. 
(c) The Indian Council of Agricultur al Research (ICAR) has.initiated 
a net-working project in 2004, to carefully monitor resistance development 
in all the 9 cotton growing States of the country and also to scientifically 
analyze all factors that contribute to  resistance development. The national 
net-working group has been given the task of developing resistance 
management strategies from time to time every year and disseminate 
them to all the stakeholders, incl uding the Genetic Engineering Approval 
Committee (GEAC), the State agricultural universities, Government 
institutions, farmers, Non-Government al Organisation (NGO), etc. So far 
based on the simulation analysis, using the 'Bt-Adapt' model, and scientific 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
data available thus far, CICR has proposed some important resistance 
management strategies to the GEAC. The strategies place emphasis on reducing 
populations of H. armigera that survive Bt. cotton and enhancement of area of 
alternate host crop that are as attractive as cotton to H. armigera, to be used as 
trap crop or intercrop refuges. If proper pest management measures are 
followed to ensure that at least 90% of the surviving larvae of the American 
bollworms in Bt-cotton fields, are killed with biopesticides, resistance can be 
delayed to 45 years even with 40% area under Bt-cotton. The following 
strategies have been proposed to the GEAC for approval and implementations 
so as to ensure that resistance is delayed for a much longer time. The strategies, 
that would enable extending the usefulness of Bt technology would be:— 
(i) Use eco-friendly methods such as cultural control or hand-picking of 
surviving bollworms in Bt cotton fields. Deep-ploughing of fields 
immediately after Bt-cotton harvest to destroy resistant pupae. 
(ii) Biopesticides that are neem based or HaNPV (virus) were found to be 
more effective on larvae surviving on Bt-cotton because of their slower 
growth as compared to those on the conventional non-Bt cotton. Hence these 
would be useful to manage younger larvae on 60-90 days old crop. 
Alternatively, eco-friendly insecticides such as spinosad, emamectin 
benzoate, novaluron or Indoxacarb can be used on 90 and 120 days old crop to 
reduce populations of resistant inset genotypes. 
(iii) Use of attractive synchronous alternate host crops such as 
marigold, sunflower, chillies etc. for H. armigera which could be used as 
intercrop or trap crop refuges. 
(iv) Use alternate genes that do not share common resistance 
mechanisms as that of CrylAc, in tran sgenic plants either in rotation or 
alternation or mixtures such as the dual-gene based Bt-cotton varieties.

Food Prize for his work to enhance nutrition for over 1 million people 
through the expansion of aquaculture and fish farming in South and South-
East Asia. Through his. "dedicated sust ained efforts in Bangladesh, Laos and 
other countries in South-East Asia", Dr. Gupta has been selected as the 2005

nutrition and wellbeing". Dr. Gupta developed unique method offish farming, 
requiring little cost while causing no environmental damage. As a result, 
freshwater fish production has risen dramatically in these countries by as much

(FFDAs). As a result, the average p ond productivity in fish farming has

514. SHRI RAMA MUNI RE DDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have simplified the drug pricing 
through a notification in the month of January, 2005; 
(b) the details of drugs that are going to be available at a lesser prices 
as a result of the present move: 
(c) whether the price of life-saving drugs will also come down due to 
simplification of drug prices; and 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
(d) if so, the details of drugs that are going to become cheap? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) Drugs and medicines have been brought under the 
levy of excise duty on the basis of retail price, vide notification No. 2/2005-
Central Excise (NT) dated 7.1.2005. For this purpose, 35% on retail price had 
been provided as abatement, i.e. the excise duty was made chargeable on 65% 
of the retail price. Subsequently, the Government has revised the abatement 
level to 40% vide Notification No. 4/2005-Central Excise (N.T.) dated 
23.2.2005. 
(b) to (d) Prior to 8.1.2005, drugs and medicines were leviable to excise 
duty on ad valorem basis and the duty was levied on the basis of transaction 
value ex-factory. There were wide variation between ex-factory prices (assessable 
value) and the declared retail price of drugs, which led to valuation disputes. 
Retail price based levy of excise duty is to facilitate assessment and provides 
uniformity. The change in the mode of assessment of excise duty on drugs is 
not expected to have an impact on the retail prices of drugs and medicines. 
Margin on Drugs 
515.    SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether, according to a study conducted by Government, the Pharma 
Companies are giving 1000 per cent margin on some of the drugs such as 
Nimesulide, Omeprozol, Cetrizine, etc.; 
(b) if so, what the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority is doing in 
this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Sandhu Committee has been constituted to look 
into all these aspects; and 
(d) if so, what are the recommendations made by the Committee? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) The Drugs  (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 1995) was promulgated by the Government vide S.O.18(E) dated 
6.1.1995. The 74 bulk drugs specified in its First Schedule and the 
80 

[29 July, 2005J RAJYA SABHA 
formulations based thereon are under price control and their prices are 
fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in 
accordance with the pr ovisions of the DPCO, 1995. These drugs have been 
identified for inclusion under price control in the DPCO, 95, on the basis of 
criteria mentioned in the "Modifications in Drug Policy, 1986,' announced in 
September, 1994. These criteria take into account the extent of usage and the 
market competition of various drugs. 
Cetrizine Nimesulide and Omeprazole are non-Scheduled formulations. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the vari ous factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government takes 
corrective measures when the public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
NPPA has collected data on trade margin being offered by the 
manufacturers to the retailers for a limited sample. It was noted that some 
manufacturers had offered high margin to the retailers, however, the market 
share of such medicines was small. 
(c) and (d) The Government constituted a Committee, on 19th August, 
2004 under the Chairmanship of Joint Secretary (PI) to examine the span of 
price control (including trade margin) in the light of National Common 
Minimum Programme. 
This Committee has submitted its interim report to the Government. The 
Committee has recommended, inter-alia, intensive monitoring on the prices 
of all those drugs out of the selected basket (National List of Essential 
Medicines, 2003) which are not under price control, ceilings on trade margins of 
drugs, a system of price negotiations for the new patented drugs, special schemes 
for people below poverty line, introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line 
Fluid Stores (hospital pharmacy stores run by Medicare Societies) for bulk 
purchase of drugs directly from manufacturer and selling them at reduced 
prices, compounding of offences under the Essential Commodities Act, 
establishment of DPCO cells in all States on the model of Karnataka, price 
negotiations at the time of launching of a new patented drug, efforts to 
increase public awareness, wide publicity to policies and decisions of the 
Government and NPPA etc. Follow up action has been initiated on the 
recommendations of the Committee made in its interim report.

Ministry of Commerce & Industry and other Ministries concerned, to stop

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) The Central 
Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has initiated stops to prepare a Manual on 
assessing e-waste in the country, for wh ich the work has been awarded to a

(c) and (d) Electronic waste is included under List-A and List-B of 
Schedule-3 of the Hazardous Waste (Management & Handling) Rules, 1989 as 
amended in 2000 and 2003. E-waste is also regulated by the Basel 
Convention on the Control of Trans-Boundary Movement of Hazardous 
Waste and their Disposal. No country can export e-waste without written 
consent from the importing country. The import of this waste, therefore, 
requires specific permission of the Ministry of Environment & Forests. No 
such permission has been given to any authority or person by the Ministry till 
date for import of e-waste. 
As per the Foreign Trade Policy 2004-2009, import of second hand 
computers is under the restricted category and their import requires an import 
licence. Such second hand computers ar e allowed to be imported for use in 
educational institutions, NGOs and charitable organisations of the country. 
Import licences are granted with the approval of an Inter-Ministerial Committee 
of the Directorate General of Forei gn Trade (DGFT). As per the available 
information, the quantity of second hand computers, etc., permitted for import 
so far being small, the same does not form major constituent of e-waste in the 
country.

Statements 
Revised guidelines for Wildlife Tourism (1998) 
In pursuance of the decision taken in the Meeting of the Standing 
Committee of the Indian Board for Wildlife held on 5.11.97, a Committee 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
was formed to further develop and revise the guidelines for wildlife tourism which had been 
developed in 1994. The Constitution of the Committee was as follows: 
1. Dr. M.K. Ranjitsinh Chairperson 
2. Shri D.S. Chavda Member 
3. Shri Mahender Vyas Member 
4. Shri C.R.V. Rao Member 
5. Shri Surender Kumar Member 
The Committee met on 30th Jan. and 18th Feb., 99. Shri C.R.V. Rao, Deputy 
Director General, Ministry of Tourism, attended the second meeting only. The 
Committee drew up the following report regarding wildlife tourism. 
1. Rationale for policy on wildlife tourism 
The. Committee felt that the foremost and the basic principle to govern wildlife 
tourism should be that the Protected Areas are not for tourism but tourism must be for 
Protected Areas. Primacy of conservation over commerce should be the guiding force in 
drawing a tourism plan for any protected area. 
It should be noted that the tourism must complement and be subservient to 
conservation and it should in no way pose a threat to or be derogatory to the conservation 
efforts of the country in general and the Protected Areas, in particular. However, it is also to 
be noted that tourism can be a potent force to help conserve the protected area and this 
must be taken advantage of. In the development of wildlife tourism the emphasis should be on 
the inculcation of conservation values, empathy for animals and communion with nature 
and not merely a satisfaction of curiosity with the mega species nor should it become 
mere picnic jaunts. While direct tourism management by the park authorities may not be 
feasible and would also be a drain on time and other resources of the park authorities, 
however they should have a final say in all matters relating to tourism in the park. 
It has been observed that the areas which are most frequently visited by tourists also 
happen to be the areas which offer best wildlife viewing. 
114 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
This may partly be due to tourists going to the best wildlife areas of the 
Protected Area but is also a fact that tourist movement provides protection leading 
to increase in wildlife. Therefore properly regulated tourism can and should play 
a positive role in ensuring long term survival of the wildlife. 
The Committee also noted that there should be harmony between the 
Wildlife Action Plan of the country, which is under revision, with the revised 
guidelines on tourism. Similarly, the Wildlife (Protection) Act which is in process 
of being amended should also be consistent with these. 
Revised Guidelines: 
1. Each Protected area must have its own tourism plan in a certain 
time frame, say one year, the essence of  which should also find place in 
the overall management plan of the Protected Area. The Plan should 
clearly indicate the area open to tour ism and closed to tourism. For any 
sizeable Protected Area, particularly t hose where tourist pressure is high, 
steps should be taken to alleviate tourist pressure by developing Satellite 
tourism zones, preferably in the buffe r areas. If this is not feasible to 
develop in a reasonable period of time, certain areas could be earmarked 
within existing protected areas, prefer ably on the periphery so that visit 
to these areas will lead to better pr otection and, therefore, enhancement 
of wildlife. 
Not only are our protected areas rath er small in size but the problem is 
further compounded by the over-conneciion of tourists in small pockets within 
these protected areas, mainly in relation to the presence of mega species. This 
has to be curbed and a more equitable distribution of tourists is to be achieved. 
As it is observed that there is a concentration of tourists only in a 
certain part of the year, measures should also be taken to distribute the tourists 
pressure by offering incentives during the off-season when the protected area 
is stilt open for the visitors. 
2. The core area of the protected areas should be clearly demarcated 
and protected as a Sanctum-sanctorum. No tourism at all should be 
allowed in this zone. However, permission to visit these "off limit" areas 
should be given to research workers and wildlife experts in the lamer 
interests of the protected area after due consideration by the authorities. 
Special and distinct passes should be issued for this purpose. 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
3. There should be a ceiling on the number of visitors allowed to enter a 
protected area at any time of the given pa rt of the year. This number has to be 
determined by the Park authorities in terms of carrying capacity, available 
facilities, transport and gu ides. The most effective method to achieve this 
objective would be by restricting both the number of vehicles entering a protected 
area and the number of vehicles permitted to visit a special area within that 
protected area at a given time. This aspect which is already in vogue is some 
areas of India and abroad will have to have a much wider application in our 
protected areas. 
4. To avoid large number of tourists staying inside the forest, day-trippers should 
be allowed inside the protected areas but they should not be permitted "picnics" 
which could result in danger to the tourists, disturbance to wildlife littering, fires 
and other hazards to the habitat. Routes of day-trippers should pre-determined 
and may need to be somewhat different from overnight visitors to avoid 
interest clashed. 
The area where visitors can get o ff from their vehicles should be 
specially earmarked with signboards. 
Day-trippers and other tourists should be able to obtain permits in 
advance to prevent rush at the entry points. 
5. An interpretation centre adequately equipped with maps, guides, 
books and audio-visual aids should be  set up at the entrance so as to 
provide nature education and proper orie ntation to visitors. This will also 
enabie the visitors to develop the right attitude before they enter the 
protected areas. However, trained personnel should be provided at the 
visitors centre failing which the centre may end up as a static facility. 
Check lists of flora and fauna including avi-fauna should be prepared and 
made available to the visitors at a suitable price. 
6. it is oDserved that the guidelines, norms and rules are mainly flouted by the 
public servants and agencies. This has to be overcome both in the interest of 
the Park authorities as well as for the purpose of fairness and equity. Normal 
rules and rates for accommodation, vehicle etc. must apply to all such visitors 
who visit the park except for the officials involved with the management of the 
park. 
7. Cooking of meals or carrying of transistors, musical instruments, 
loudspeakers or any arms or weapons inside the sanctuary by any visitor inside 
the protected area should be strictly prohibited. 
116 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
8. As tourism is now being recognized as an industry and is one of the fastest 
growing sector of the economy; Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) of the 
more important protected areas should be undertaken from the viewpoint of 
impact of tourism. 
9. All new accommodation for the tourists including related infrastructure as 
cafeteria, shops etc. must be located outside the protected area. Such new 
accommodation etc. should be in a corner of the buffer area in a wild setting 
with natural surroundings around, the design and ambience should reflect the 
concerns of authentic wildlife tourism. Similarly expansion of existing 
accommodation and other tourist facilities within the protected area should not 
be permitted. 
 
10. The motorized Conveyance used should be low noise and should also 
carrying Pollution Under Control Certif icate (PUC). Even cyclists and 
trekking in small groups should be allowed on approved routes in designated 
areas of buffer zones where there is no danger from carnivores and wild elephants. 
Vehicles should not be allowed to drive off the designates trekkers and the 
visitors traveling in them should step  out only in certain designated places. 
Tarring and even re-tarring of roads should not be allowed inside the 
protected area. 
11. Entry of tourists to the protected ar eas including the vehicles will have 
to be on payment of required fees which should have a graded structure, the 
highest being for the foreign tourists and the lowest for the students. A brochure 
containing the map of the protected area and a list of dos and don'ts inside the 
park should be given with the entry permit and the cost recovered. 
12. All revenues from the protected area must be ploughed back and should 
not accrue to the State exchequer. Provision should also be made for setting up 
of donation boxes clearly indicating that the money so obtained would be used 
for the betterment of the park and for the welfare of the park staff/local 
inhabitants. 
13. Rates for use of cameras for photography inside the protected areas should 
be drawn up in a rational manner so that it does not discourage the wildlife 
lovers to visit the protected areas and document their observation. The rates for 
use of cameras for commercial purpose should be much higher than the personal 
photography taken by individuals for the remembrance of their visit. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
14. The tourist guides and tour operators should be given adequate 
orientation and training programme so th at they are able to pass on correct 
information and an appropriate value sy stem to the customers they guide. 
Very often the tourists' behave in a manner detrimental to conservation 
because they are not properly brie fed about the "Dos and Don'ts" or 
even sometimes wrongly briefed about some exciting incidents. 
The nature guides would have to obtain a permit from the park 
authorities which would be periodically renewed based on the performance of the 
guides. The local people should be encouraged and trained to perform as 
nature guides, however under no circumstances the park staff should be used 
as guides. The fee that should be payable to the guides should also be fixed by 
the Park authorities. 
15. Small controlled educational camps may also be organized in earmarked 
areas outside of the sanctuary or national park for staying in tents with a strict 
code of conduct for occupation of such tents and maintenance of camping 
sites. 
16. AH tourism structures that come up in  the fringe of the protected areas 
or in the periphery should blend in with the surroundings, be moderately 
priced, clean and wholesome. This is necessary to offer as "near to nature" an 
experience to visitors as possible. 
17. In certain protected areas government may consider declaring "No 
development zone" under the Environment (Protection) Act, where 
development, including tourism is likely to create an adverse impact. 
18. The water and energy needs of a protected area should be met from 
outside. Use of non polluting alternative energy sources should be encouraged. 
Use of fuel wood should be prohibited in all tourist facilities, including private. 
19. It should be ensured that the visitors do not dispose of non 
biodegradable waste inside the protected area. Even otherwise proper 
arrangement should exist for the disposal of all the garbage. 
20. Surrounding and chivying of the wild animals by vehicles and elephants 
which lead to stress for the animals should not be allowed. 
21. In many of the Protected Areas pl aces of worship and reverence exist 
which are visited by large number of people. Steps should be taken 
118 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to ensure that commerce does not take precedence here as this would neither 
be in the interest of conservation nor in maintaining the sanctity and tranquility 
of the place of worship. Efforts should also be made to mitigate the impact of 
pilgrims in consultation with the management of the religious places. 
No new places of worship should be allowed to come up nor expansion 
of existing places should be allowed inside the protected areas. 
Statement II 
Regulation of Tourist Visitation in Tiger Reserves Dated: 9th April, 2003 
F.No. PS(DIR)—PT  
To, 
Field Director 
(All Tiger Reserves) 
SUBJECT: Regulation of Tourist Visitation in Tiger Reserves 
Sir, 
As you are aware, there is consider able tourist influx (both inland and 
foreign) in many of our Protected Areas and Tiger Reserves, which necessitate 
regulation of such visitation in the interest of minimizing the biotic disturbance 
to wild animals and their habitat. It must be borne in mind, ecotourism should 
be fostered in the right perspective in these areas, so that there is no 
compromise or trade-off in wildlife in terests, since our Tiger Reserves are 
ecotypical repositories of valuable gene pool. Hence, the following may be 
ensured in this regard: 
• The tourist visitation should be regulated as per the carrying capacity of the 
area. 
• In place of open gypsies and smaller ve hicles, medium sized buses, with a 
closed body and sliding windows, may be used for park excursions. This 
will minimize the risk of close encounters with wild 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
animals, apart from reducing the number of vehicles inside the park at any 
point in time. 
• A minimum mandatory distance of at least 500 meters should be 
maintained between two vehicles plying on the same road. 
• A minimum mandatory distance of 30 meters should be maintained by 
•tourist vehicles while spotting a tiger or any other wild animal. 
• The route guides should be more professionally trained and penalty 
should be imposed on visitors in case they violate park rules. 
Further, a model calculation of the Tourist Carrying Capacity is also 
appended for ready reference, which is fairly robust and can be computed in a site-
specific manner by collecting some basic field data. It is requested, this computation 
may please be done for your Reserve and this Ministry may be apprised 
accordingly. Since a certain amount of risk is always involved in jungle 
excursions despite all precautions, a standardized 'Indemnity Bond' may also be 
prescribed indemnifying the park authorities from litigation/arbitration which may 
arise on account of accidents suffered by tourists during park round. All due 
formalities in this regard may be completed before the tourists are allowed 
entry into the Tiger Reserve. Under no circumstances tourist excursions should 
be allowed during the night. It goes without saying, apart from causing immense 
disturbance to wild animals, such vent ures are extremely risky. It is also 
reiterated, no tourist facilities should be created in the 'core Zone' of a Tiger 
Reserve. 
Yours Sincerely, 
Dr. Rajesh Gopal

574. SHRI S. M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether ICMR has done any studies on the growing prevalence of 
diabetes amongst the younger people in India; 
(b) if so, the findings of this study; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
150 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) to what extent has the study shown that soft drinks; sugar based food, 
fast food are the primary causes of diabetes amongst our youth; 
(d) whether Government have made awareness schemes to counter this 
trend of sickness amongst our youth; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) It is 
estimated that number of diabetics in the country is 32 million of which 
roughly 10% is insulin dependent diabetes of the young as reported by WHO. 
A hospital based study on south Indian urban population reported that 32.6% of 
their 11359 patients developed Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM) at 
<15 years of age. A population based study in Chennai found prevalence of 
IDDM in 0.26% per 1000 in <15 yrs. with a major peak at 12 years. A study 
was conducted by the Delhi Diabetes Research Centre, a non-governmental 
organisation in collaboration with Govt, of Delhi, focusing on hazards of obesity 
and its relation with diabetes, among the school children in Delhi. The study 
concluded that lack of physical activ ity/exercise comb ined with excess 
consumption of fast food and aerated drinks is the major cause of over weight 
obesity in these children which may be a pre-disposing factor towards diabetes. 
Under an ongoing ICMR-WHO study on Non-communicable Disease (NCD) 
surveillance, the diabetes as a risk factor of NCD has been taken up in the age 
group of 15-64 years at Delhi, Dibrugarh, Trivandrum, Chennai and Nagpur. 
This study will also provide prevalence of diabetes in young age group. 
Since creating awareness throug h information, education and 
communication is the main strategy to tackle this issue, this component has 
been incorporated in the National Pr ogramme for Control of Diabetes and 
Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD) for which this Ministry has sought in principle 
approval from the Planning Commission.

Safe blood to patients 
577. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACH ARJEE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to provide safe blood to 
patients needing blood transfusion besides AIDS patients; and 
(b) if so, whether the patients will be required to pay for the blood? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATi PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The' 
Government is already implementing a scheme to provide and adequate quantity 
of safe blood, blood components and blood products to the needy citizens. As one 
of the routes for transmission of HIV/AIDS is through blood transfusion, the 
Government has included Blood Safety as a major component under National 
AIDS Control Programme. Since the 'commencement of the First phase of the 
programme in 1992, the Government undertook a major task for modernizing 
and strengthening all blood banks in the Government sector and some in the 
voluntary and charitable sectors. 
154 
 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Subsequently, a National Blood Policy (NBP) was formulated by 
National AIDS Control Organisation, and adopted by the Government in April 
2002. It provides a framework for better management and availability of safe 
blood and blood products in the country. This was followed up with a detailed 
Action Plan on Blood Safety with clear articulation of steps to implement the 
policy. 
(b) No charges are leviable for blood as it is collected from voluntary and 
replacement donors who are not paid for donating blood. However, the donated 
units are subjected to mandatory screening of transfusion transmitted diseases, 
blood grouping and cross-matching, before it is issued for transfusion to the 
patients. Hence a subsidized service charge of Rs. 250/- is recovered for each 
unit of safe and screened blood by Government and Voluntary Blood Banks. 
But patients suffering from thalassemia and hemophilia are exempted even 
from these service charges in the entire country.

increase in TB Cases 
579. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Tuberculosis (T.B.) cases have increased 
many folds in the recent past; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the deaths on account of Tuberculosis have 
also increased; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefore; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that required attention nas not been given to 
this disease and much attention is being given to disease like AIDS etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The number 
of TB cases reported under National TB Control Programme (NTCP) have 
been more or less static during last few years. As per latest ARTI survey (2000-
03), the incidence of new sputum positive cases is 75/lakh population as 
compared to 85/lakh prior to year 2000. 
(b) Consequent upon implementation of Revised National TB Control 
Programme (RNTCP) since 1997, currently covering about 1030 million 
population, treatment success rate has tripled from 25% to 85% and death rate 
has been cut 7 fold from 29% to about 4% among patients registered under 
RNTCP. As per WHO latest estimates, death rate due to TB has declined from 
45/lakh in 1990 to 33/lakh in 2003. 
(c) Does not arise. 
(d) No, Sir. Adequate attention is also being given to TB Control 
activities in the country. 
Revised National TB control Programme (RNTCP), widely known as 
DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, with the objective of 
achieving cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and to detect at least 
70% of such cases, is being implemented since year 1997 in a phased manner 
as a 100% Centrally sponsored Scheme. 
Presently, about 1030 million population in more than 575 districts/ 
reporting units has been covered under the revised strategy, it is proposed to cover 
the entire country under the programme during the current year.

†585. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the number of AIDS patients in India has 
reached over 50 lakhs as per a report of World Bank; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government to check its spread as an 
epidemic, create awareness about it and to make available the resources to 
infected persons; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

(c) the results achieved so far through the efforts made by

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) No, Sir. The 
World Bank has published a report titled "HIV/AIDS Treatment and 
Prevention in India" in June 2004. There is no mention that the number of 
AIDS patients in India has reached over 50 lakhs. 
However, National AIDS Control Organization, Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, conducts annual round of HIV sentinel surveillance in 
designated sentinel sites all over the country. One such round was conducted 
in 2004 from July to September 2004. Based on this set of data, it is estimated 
that there are 51.34 lakh HIV infections in the country. The number of AIDS 
cases reported by the States/UTs till 31st March, 2005 is 1,03,857. 
(b) In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, 
Govt, of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme under following components:- 
• Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through 
targeted interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including 
peer counseling and behaviour change communication. 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing 
services, Pervention of Parent to Child Transmission (PPTCT), 
Information Education and Communication (IEC). 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. Free ART services have also 
been started from 2004-05 through selected hospitals. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme 
activities including workplace interventions and public-private 
partnerships.

♦ Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and 
Evaluation, Technical Resource Groups, operational research 
and Programme management. 
(c) Various achievements made under National AIDS Control 
Programme are as follows: 
♦ National AIDS Prevention & Control Policy and National Blood 
Policy are in place, to prevent the epidemic from further spread and 
reduce the socio-economic impact. 
♦ State AIDS Control Societies have been constituted at State/ UT 
level as an autonomous body for implementation of programme 
activities. 
♦ To ensure early diagnosis and management of sexually transmitted 
diseases (STD), 735 STD clinics are supported by providing 
necessary consumables and drugs. 
♦ 804 Voluntary Counselling Tes ting Centers are already in 
existence, in order to provide access to people for voluntary HIV 
testing with pre and post test counseling. 
♦ Free Antiretro-viral therapy is being provided in 25 centres in 
public sector hospitals. 
♦ 965 Targeted Intervention projects are implemented through Non 
Governmental Organisations to prevent HIV spread among high-risk 
populations. 
♦ In order to provide care for term inally ill patients suffering from 
HIV/AIDS, 51 community care centers have been established in 
high prevalent States. 
♦ 307 PPTCT centres are providi ng a package of services for 
preventive intervention for transmission from HIV infected 
mothers to their children. 
♦ Provision of one functional Blood Bank in each district to ensure safety 
of blood and blood products. 1020 blood banks are persently 
supported under the programme.

♦ 670 sentinel sites were established in identified clinics and 
Targetted Intervention projects to track progression of HIV

with HIV/AIDS, financial support is being provided to major hospitals 
in all States/UTs of the Country.

FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have imposed a ban on the sale of non-iodised 
salt in the country;  
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the difference in the cost of iodised and non-iodised salt for the 
consumer; 
(d) the names of companies which are marketing iodised salt in the 
country; 
(e) whether a large number of people are against this ban on non-iodised 
salt; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) The 
Government of India has taken a decision to restrict the sale of edible 
common salt for direct human consumption unless it is iodized. However, it may 
be sold for iodization, iron fortification, animal use, preservation, 
manufacturing medicines and industrial use under proper label declaration.

iodized salt and non-iodized salt is marginal, because the cost of iodization is 
only approx. 10 paise per Kg and thus its percentage contribution to the retail 
price is negligible.

registered with Salt Department engaged in the production and marketing of 
iodized salt in the country.

human consumption without furnishing scientific evidence on the

harmful effects of iodisation of salt. However, the Government decision which

experts as well as the World Health Organization and UNICEF as a measure

retardation and lowered IQ in growing children. At present, 92 countries in the

New AIDS vaccine 
592. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Hadassa University Medical Centre 
of Israel has developed a vaccine for HIV/AIDS for first time; 
(b) if so, the details of the research done by Hadassa University; and 
(c) what exactly is the difference betw een AIDS cocktail medicine that 
is now being given to patients and the vaccine developed by the said University? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes 
Sir, it has been reported that an Israeli research team at Hadassah Medical Center has 
developed a vaccine, and it has been claimed that it strengthen body's immune 
system against the auto-immune aftereffects of HIV infection. The Hadassah 
study was conducted between 1998—2002  with an additional two-year 
monitoring period. Seven patients participated in the study out of which five 
responded positively to the vaccine. Extended Clinical trails are yet to be 
conducted. However, the Government of India has not received any official 
information so far. 
(c) The AIDS Cocktail medicine ar e basically different triple drug 
combinations, that have been shown to improve the quality of life as well 
prolong the life. It is also known as Highly Active Anti Retroviral Therapy 
(HAART). Israeli vaccine only complements HAART. However, as the study 
was conducted only on seven patients ther efore, extended clinical trial are 
needed before commenting upon its effectiveness.

(b) to (d) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its judgement dated 14.8.03 in the 
case of Islamic Academy of Education has clarified that the State Government 
may prescribe the percentage of seats in private professional colleges which can 
be filled by the management. The remain ing seats are to be filled up as per 
merit through the common entrance test conducted by the state agency. The 
seats filled by the management are also to be filled up as per merit through a 
common entrance test to be conducted by the association of all colleges in the 
concerned State or in the absence of such association, by the common entrance

been clarified that each in stitution shall have the freedom to fix its own fee 
structure. Each State Government is required to set up a Committee under the 
Chairmanship of a retired High Court Judge to decide whether the fee proposed 
by the institute is justified and does not amount to profiteering or charging of 
capitation fee. The said Committee may approve the fee structure proposed by 
the institute or may propose some other fee which shall be binding on the 
institute for a period of three years.

colleges. All the admissions are done on th e basis of merit as per the result of

Direct Monitoring System for Spurious Medicines 
604. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the role of Government in curbei ng the manufacture of spurious 
medicines and drugs at manufacturing level and at the level of 
pharmaceutical distributors; 
(b) whether Government would enact any law for directly creating and 
monitoring vigilance system throughout India to curb the ever growing menace of 
spurious medicines and drugs worth several thousands of crores of rupees 
without being controlled by States; 
(c) if so, the details of the proposed law; and 
(d) if not, the measures Government would propose for its direct 
involvement to curb this ever growing menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a)to(d) Under 
the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules thereunder, it is the 
responsibility of State Governments through their respective Drug Control 
organizations to regulate manufacture and sale of drugs as well as to keep a 
surveillance over possible movement of spurious/counterfeit drugs. 
Manufacture and sale of spurious /counterfeit drugs is primarily a 
clandestine activity. To this extent, it is difficult to detect the manufacture of 
movement of spurious drugs. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
Trading in counterfeit products including drugs is reported world over. 
However, keeping in view the serious implicaitons of spurious drugs on public 
health as well as the loss to genuine industry, the Govt, has taken various 
measures to combat this menace. 
(i) Detailed guidelines have been issued to the State Govts, to 
undertake focused surveillance over possible movement of 
spurious drugs. 
(ii) A Capacity Building Project th rough World Bank assistance has. 
been taken up to provide substantial assistance to State Govts, to 
upgrade drug testing facilities and to establish new drug testing 
laboratories. 
It is expected to increase the number of samples tested in the country 
from about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per year and to 
reduce the reporting time to less than a month as against the present 
period from 3 to 6 months. 
(iii) Specific training programme fo r regulatory officials of State 
Govts, on logistics of intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been 
conducted with the assi stance of FDA, Mahara shtra. This is an 
ongoing activity. 
(iv) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug 
regulatory officers in the coun try, in respect of licensing, 
sampling, prosecution, etc., a co untrywide computer networking 
project has been undertaken by the Central Govt. This will enable 
the Central Govt, to regularly monitor the enforcement activities 
and recommend corrective measures. 
(v) Pharma industry and trade has been motivated to fight menace of 
spurious drugs as a shared responsibility. No of cases could be 
successfully detected through the initiative taken by Pharma 
industry involving hiring of retired intelligence officers. 
(vi) The recommendation of Mashelkar Committee which was 
constituted by the Government in 2003, to examine all aspects 
relating to the drug regulatory system in the country including the 
problem of spurious/sub standard drugs, are being followed for 
necessary change in legislation as well as improvement of 
enforcement activities. 
190 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2005 has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha in May, 2005 to amend the said 
Act to provide for stricter penalities to the offenders including a 
maximum penalty of life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 100,000/-
. It further proposes to make the offence non-bailable, c ognizable 
and to provide for specially designated courts for speedy trial of 
the cases. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders 
involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of 
enforcing agencies like Police will help in speedy investigation to book the 
culprits and in controlling anti-social elements in such activities.

Rising gap between male-female ratio in the country 
609. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite so many laws and regulations 
existing in the country, gap between male-female ratio is on the rise; 
(b) if so, the details of steps taken to ameliorate the situation; and 
(c) the reasons for the non-conviction in the past few years in the cases 
of charges of misuse of diagnostic techniques by various nursing homes and 
clinics? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The female 
to male ratio declined in India from 972 in 1901 to 927 in 1991. However, the 
sex ratio has since improved to 933 as per 2001 Census. 
(b) The Pre-conception and Pre- natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act,  1994 (PC & PNDT Act) is being 
implemented in the country. The Act provides for the prohibition of sex 
selection, before or after conception, and for regulation of pre-natal diagnostic 
techniques for the purpose of detecting certain abnormalities and for the 
prevention of their misuse for sex determination leading to female foeticide; 
and for the matters connected therewith. The Implmentation of the Act rests with 
the States and Union Territories through the Appropriate Authorities appointed 
under the Act at State, District as well at Sub-district levels. It is, nevertheless, 
recognized that mere PC & PNDT Act is not enough to deal with the problem 
that has roots in social behavior and prejudices. Various activities have been 
undertaken to create awareness against the practice of pre-natal determination 
of sex and female foeticide through Radio, Television, and print media. 
Workshops and seminars have also been organized at 
State/regional/district/block levels to create awareness against this social evil. 
Cooperation has also been sought from NGOs, religious/spiritual leaders, as 
well as medical fraternity to curb this practice. The Government of India has 
launched 'Save the Girl Child Campaign' with a view to lessen son preference 
by 
197 

RAJYA SABHA                          [29 July, 2005] 
highlighting achievements of young girls. A National Inspection and 
Monitoring Committee with members from National commission for Women, 
Department of women and Child Development, and reputed NGOs has been 
constituted to take stock of the situation at ground level by visiting clinics in 
States/UTs. 
(c) The Pre-conception and Pre- natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (PC & PNDT Act) was amended in 
2003 and is being implemented in the country. At present, 308 court cases are 
filed in courts in various states and Union Territories. The clinics are inspected for 
violation of the Act and action to suspend the registration is taken by the 
Appropriate Authorities. One of the problems is that the activity of sex 
determination takes place secretly where both the service providers and service 
seekers are in league to defeat the provisions of the law.

pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to improve various goods transport 
facilitation rail network in the next five years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken or proposed to be taken for 
generating additional rail capacity for carrying long and short haul bulk goods by 
making it industry and consumer friendly; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Japan International Co-operation Agency has offered 
financial assistance for Mumbai-Delhi and Mumbai-Kolkata rail corridor project; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof?

VELU): (a) and (b) Improvement and expansion of the Rail 
219

network is a continuous and ongoing exercise. Every year as part of the Budget 
exercise works relating to New Lines,  Gauge Conversion, Doubling, Traffic 
Facilities, etc. are sanctioned for improvement of the goods transport facilities 
as well as expansion of the physical rail network. During the 10th Plan (2002-07) 
it has been envisaged to add 1310 Kms. of New Lines, 2365 Kms. of Gauge 
Conversion and 1500 Kms. of Doubling for expansion of the Rail network. An 
Integrated Railway Modernization Plan (2005-2010) has been formulated for 
overall improvement in the facilities in the rail network including various 
measures to improve running of freight trains on Golden Quadrilateral and its

634. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Wiil the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a serious track breach occured between Warangal and 
Hyderabad due to rains recently;

(c) whether Railways have not selected proper routes to ensure that rain water 
does not impact tracks or local topography; 
(d) the steps to be taken to study on what system the Railways should follow to 
ensure that rain water and flooded rivers do not harm local people; and

are built beneath tracks to avoid creating floods by the Railways? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Due to heavy rains on 09-07-05, two irrigation tanks on the 
upstream side of the track failed resulting in breaches of railway track for the length of 150 
metres between Ghanapur and Nashkal stations on Secunderabad-Kazipet section. 
Two irrigation tanks, namely Rajavaram tank situated about 3.5 km from the 
Railway track and Chinnapendiyal tank situated at about 0.3 kms on the upstream side 
had breached as a result of sudden rise in inflow into these tanks, due to breaches of 
several smaller tanks on upstream sides of these tanks. Consequently, water gushed 
towards the railway track resulting in water over flowing the railway track causing 
breaches.

(c) and (d) Railway alignments are selected after careful topographical 
and route surveys and suitably designed railway bridges are provided along the lines to 
facilitate the discharge of runoff water from catchment areas and rivers. 
The construction of river training works and protection works along river banks to 
protect local population from flooding is done by the State Governments. A number of 
Railway Affecting Works like tanks and reservoirs are constructed by the State 
Government/local authorities subsequently the breach of which may endanger the 
safety of railway tracks besides affecting the local people. A system of joint inspection of 
such Railway Affecting Works by Railways and State Government officials is set up and the 
concerned authorities are advised of measures required to be taken by them in 
advance. 
(e) During laying of railway line adequate number of bridges, culverts, openings etc.

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER 
His recent Official Visit to the United States of America 
THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am 
honoured to present to this House a stat ement on my recent visit to the United 
States. President Bush invited me to pay an official visit and my wife and I were 
received by President Bush and the First Lady Mrs. Laura Bush with great 
warmth and with full ceremonial honours. My talks with the President covered a 
wide range of bilateral and global issues. The Vice President and senior Cabinet 
members of the US Administration such as Secretary of State Dr. Condoleezza 
Rice, Defence Secretary Mr. Rumsfeld and Treasury Secretary Mr. Snow also 
called on me during my stay. 1 had the honour to be invited to address the Joint 
Session of the US Congress. I believe that the visit was a success in furthering 
our foreign policy interests and in te rms of its substantive outcome. It was 
evident that the United States wished to signal that we are embarking on a 
transformation of our ties so as to realize their inherent potential. A copy of the 
Joint Statement issued during my visit has been placed on the Table of the 
House. 
The purpose of my visit was to sensitise the US Government about the full 
extent of the changes that have taken place in India since 1991. These changes 
have given us a stronger capability to wo rk with the United States on more 
equal terms as we address common concerns and challenges. I also sought to 
emphasise that the Indian economy is stronger than it has ever been and we 
hope to participate in and benefit from the economic processes of globalisation. 
We are determined to be a competitive destination for investment, including 
foreign investment and the US business community could contribute to 
development in India through greater investment and trade. We are uniquely 
placed to enter into such mutually beneficial interaction drawing on the 
strength of our knowledge sector. Hence another important goal was to underline 
to the US that the emergence of India as a centre of knowledge based industries 
and services would provide a good basis for long-term collaboration between 
our two economies. The expansion of the Indian economy and acceleration of 
our growth rases is crucial not just for own people but would be beneficial to 
global economic progress and stability as well. 
My discussions in Washington with President Bush and members of his 
Administration were productive and helped advance these national 
254 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
goals. Both sides agreed that our relationship was based on shared values and shared 
interests that included the strengthening of democratic capacities where desired and 
without coercion, and in combating terrorism without selectivity or segmentation. The 
conclusion of the UN Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism proposed by 
India, at an early date, was deemed a priority by both countries. On the economic side, we 
welcomed the launching of a CEOs Forum that has brought together the best business 
minds of both countries. We discussed the urgent need for modernization of India's 
infrastructure and our quest for greater investments in this sector, in view of its centrality for 
the continued growth of the indian economy. Recognizing the importance of the rural 
economy, we also agreed on an agricultural initiative aimed at facilitating a new generation 
of research and agricultural practices to build on the green revolution. 
Appreciating the importance of technology to India's economic and social 
development, we also discussed measures that would ensure more liberal and predictable 
access to US high technology. We will endeavour to build closer ties in frontier areas such 
as space exploration, satellite navigation and launch, and related commercial activities that 
would greatly benefit our space industry, which is recognized today as a global leader. 
AScience and Technology framework Agreement has been agreed during my visit that 
provides for expanded joint research and training. Underlining the intent of working at a new 
level of cooperation, the United States announced the removal of five Indian 
organizations from its Entity List— three from the space sector and two from the atomic 
energy—and indicated further review in this matter. 
Sir, India's quest for energy security as an essential component of our vision for 
our development was a significant theme of my talks. I elaborated the imperative need for 
India to have unhindered access to ail sources of energy, including nuclear energy, if we 
are to maintain and accelerate our rate of economic growth. Sir, I am pleased to state 
that the US understood our position in regard to our securing adequate and affordable 
energy supplies, from all sources. This approach, I underlined, would enable us to reduce 
our dependence on fossil fuels. This would have concomitant advantages for all in terms 
of reduced pressure on oil prices and environmental sustainability. It was in this context 
that we affirmed the importance of cooperation in the civilian nuclear energy sector. 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
Sir, accordingly, a central element of my interaction with President Bush 
was the resumption of bilateral civilian nuclear cooperation between India and the 
United States, which has been frozen for decades. President Bush and I agreed 
that we would work towards promoting nuclear energy as a means for India to 
achieve energy security. The US side undertook to adjust its laws and policies 
domestically and to work with its friends and allies to adjust relevant 
international regimes. Full civilian nuclear energy cooperation would include, 
but not limit itself, to the expeditious consideration of fuel supplies for Tarapur. 
The US will also encourage other partners to consider similar requests 
favourably. We also obtained consideratio n of our desire to participate as full 
partners in the International Thermo Nuclear Research Project and the 
Generation IV International Forum. T hese programmes in frontier areas of 
science and technology have considerable potential for our country's and 
indeed global energy security in the future. The US agreed to consult other 
participants with a view towards India's inclusion. This is a testimony not only to the 
enormous international stature and respect achieved by our nuclear scientists 
but also recognition of their attainments. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, our nuclear pr ogramme is unique. It encompasses 
the complete range of activities that characterize an advanced nuclear power 
including generation of electricity, advanced research and development and 
our strategic programme. Our scientists have mastered the complete nuclear 
fuel cycle. The manner of the development of our programme which has been 
envisaged is predicated on our modest uranium resources and vast reserves of 
thorium. While the energy potential available in these resources is immense, we 
remain committed to the three-stage nuclear power programme, consisting of 
Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHW Rs) in the first stage, fast breeder 
reactors in the second stage and thoriu m reactors in the third stage. These 
would need sequential implement ation in an integrated m anner. Our scientists 
have done excellent work and we are progressing well on this programme as per 
the original vision outlined by Pandit jawaharial Nehru and Dr. Homi Bhabha. 
We will build on this precious heritage. 
Sir, energy is a crucial input to propel our economic growth. We have 
assessed our long-term energy resources and it is clear that nuclear power has to 
play an increasing role in our electricity generation plans. 
256 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
While our indigenous nuclear power programme based on domestic resources 
and national technological capabilities would continue to grow, there is clearly an 
urgent necessity for us to enhance nuclear power production rapidly. Our desire 
is to attain energy security to enable us to leapfrog stages of economic 
development obtained at the least possible cost. For this purpose, it would be 
very useful if we can access nuclear fuel  as well as nuclear reactors from the 
international market. Presently, this is not possible because of the nuclear 
technology restrictive regimes that operate around us. What we have now 
agreed with the US should open up the possibility of our being able to access 
nuclear fuel and nuclear power reactors and other technologies from outside to 
supplement our domestic efforts. There is also considerable concern with regard 
to global climate change arising out of C0 2 emission. Thus, we need to pursue 
clean energy technologies. Nuclear power is very important in this context as well. 
Sir, the Joint Statement recognizes that as a responsible State with 
advanced nuclear technology, India sh ould acquire the same benefits and 
advantages as other such States which have advanced nuclear technology. As 
a result we expect that the resumption of India's nuclear trade and commerce 
with the US, and globally, is an achievable goal, involving the dismantling of 
the technology denial regimes which have hitherto targeted India. 
Sir, predicated on our obtaining the same benefits and advantages as 
other nuclear powers, is the understandi ng that we shall undertake the same 
responsibilities and obligations as such countries, including the United States. 
Concomitantly, we expect the same rights and benefits. Thus we have ensured the 
principle of non-discrimination. I would like to make it very clear that our 
commitments would be conditional upon, and reciprocal to, the US fulfilling its 
side of this understanding. The Joint Statement refers to our identifying, and 
separating civilian and military nuclear facilities in a phased manner and taking 
a decision to place voluntarily civili an nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards. 
India will never accept discrimination. There is nothing in this Joint Statement that 
amounts to limiting or inhibiting our strategic nuclear weapons programme over 
which we will retain unrestricted, complete and autonomous control. 
Sir, reciprocity is key to the implementation of all the steps enumerated in 
the Joint Statement. We expect a close co-relation between 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
the actions to be taken by the United States and by India. Indian actions will be contingent at 
every stage on actions taken by the other side. Should we not be satisfied that our interests 
are fully secured, we shall not feel pressed to move ahead in a predetermined manner. 
I realize that there would be criticism in some quarters regarding aspects of the 
Joint Statement. Constructive criticism is part of the Parliamentary tradition, and I 
welcome it. This adds clarify to our debates and vibrancy to the institution of our 
democracy. I can, however, assure this August House, and through it, our nation, that my 
visit to the United States was undertaken solely with the purpose of enhancing relations 
with one of the world's pre-eminent powers, so as to widen our development 
options, it was my endeavour to expand our access to energy supplied to fuel our growth, while 
protecting our strategic interests. I believe our effort to undo some of the long-standing 
restrictive nuclear regimes will enable us to secure access to the significantly greater 
quantities of energy that we will need to spur massive growth in our industrialization 
programme. Once secured, cheap and affordable energy will enable India to leapfrog its 
current pace of economic growth, to secure the future for generations to come. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, all of us gathered together in this August House recognize that 
inspired by our freedom struggle, we have inherited a proud and patriotic tradition. Our 
commitment to work for universal nuclear disarmament so passionately espoused by Shri 
Rajiv Gandhi will remain our core concern in the long run. At the same time, I can 
assure the House that we have never made, nor will we ever make, any compromises insofar 
as our fundamental and strategic needs are concerned. Our inheritance gives us 
confidence, our experience gives us courage, and our belief gives us conviction to assert 
today that our nation stands on the threshold of an even better future. I, therefore, 
venture to think that my visit to the USA has opened up new opportunities and possibilities 
for promoting our energy security and pathways to accelerated social and economic 
development. We must all work together as a united nation to realize these opportunities 
to make India a major power house of the evolving global economy. Thank you

Demand for Revision of Royalty for Mineral Nines in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, Orissa is always mentioned as a State 
endowed with natural resources like various minerals. Still, it remains one of the poorest 
States for various reasons. 
My State, Orissa, is rich in varied and vast mineral deposits like coal, iron ore, 
manganese, bauxite, chromite, lead, mica etc. in so far as only coal deposits are 
concerned, Orissa has 24.3 per cent of the total coal deposits so far prospected in 
the country. 
But, with ail these gifts of nature and Mother-Earth, Orissa remains economically 
backward with its people suffering from poverty. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in The Chair] 
One of the reasons for this is the low rate of royalty fixed for various mineral products 
which are being mined in the State. It is coal, iron ore, limestone, dolomite and such other 
mineral, which are being used to feed various iron, steel, cement and other basic 
industries.

Even that very small amount is not paid on time and on a regular basis. I, therefore, 
request the Union government to consider revision of the relevant Act governing ana

I would specifically like to mention for amendment of Section 9(3) of the Mines and 
Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, with
