The National Commission for the Aged Bill, 2001—Contd. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. K URIAN): Further consideration of 
the motion, that is, The National Commission for the Aged Bill, 2001, moved by 
Dr. Karan Singh on the 6th May, 2005. 
On 6th May, 2005, the discussion on the Bill was concluded. Now, the 
Minister has to reply. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, I have carefully listened to the deliberations made by hon. 
Members of Parliament on 6th May, 2005.1 appreciate their concern for older 
persons. Hon. Members have raised the following main points during the course 
of the discussion on the Bill. 
The older people should have access to basic needs of life. They should 
remain integrated with their community life. The older people should be 
provided social, legal and health care. They should be given resources to 
develop their full potential. They should be able to live in dignity and security 
and be free of physical or mental abus e. A law should be made for making 
payment of maintenance allowances to the older people by their children in 
case they live unattended. The orphan homes and the oldage homes should be 
integrated. Some Members also expressed concern about the problem of 
poverty, treatment meted out to widows and the invasion of western culture as the 
root cause of breaking up of joint family system. In this regard, I would like to 
apprise the hon. Members of the House that the Government already has a 
National Policy on Older Persons, wherein all aspects concerning the aged have 
been addressed. The policy envisages State support for financial security, health 
care, shelter and other needs of the older persons so that they get 
opportunities to lead an active, productive and satisfying life. Further, in 
pursuance of the announcement of the policy, the Government has set 
278 

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
up a National Council for Older Persons, under the Chairmanship of Minsiter 
of Social Justice and Empowerment. The National Council for Older Persons 
is the highest body to advise and coordinate with the Government in the 
formulation and implementation of national policy and programmes for the 
welfare of the aged. The Council also works as a nodal point at the national 
level for redressing the grievances of the older persons and to represent their 
collective opinion to the Government. The Ministry has also set up an Inter-
Minislerial Committee headed by the Secretary. Social Justice and 
Empowerment for effective implementation of the National Policy for Older 
Persons and for taking action on the recommendations of the NCOP Further, 
the Ministry periodically reviews progress on the implementation of National Policy 
on old persons through meetings of National Council for Older Persons and the 
Inter-Ministerial Committee. Further, the Ministry supports programmes for the 
welfare of the elderly, through financial assistance to non-Governmental 
organisations under two schemes - one, an integrated programme for older 
persons and second, the scheme for assistance to Panchayati Raj institutions, 
voluntary organisations, self-help groups. Under these schemes, financial 
assistance is provided for establishing and maintaining old-age homes, day-care 
centres, mobile medical units and construction of old-age homes. The 
Government of India and the State Governments have wide range of schemes 
for the benefit of elderly persons like old-age pension, priority for subsidised 
health care, fare concession in all modes of travel and supply of foodgrains to 
the indigent senior citizens free of cost. Taking into account the various problems 
being faced by the older persons, the Government is actively consulting the 
State Governments and the Union Territories to frame a model legislation for 
promoting the maintenance, care and protection of older persons. The salient 
features of the proposed Bill, inter alia, are care including financial, housing, 
clothing and companionship, requirements from the families or the State 
Government in case of older persons living below the poverty line, protection of 
their life and property making adequate provisions for old-age pensions, setting 
up of old-age homes in each district and setting up of geriatric ward in each district 
hospital. A short write-up, containing these salient features, has been circulated 
to the State Governments and Union Territories, eliciting their views. As the 
expenditure on most of the provisions is to be met by the State Governments, an 
estimate about the financial implications of the Bill can only be made after the 
response 
279 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
from the State Government is received. Since the proposed Bill covers most of 
the problems of older persons, as highlighted by the hon. Members, I request 
the hon. Member of Parliament, Dr. Karan Singh, to kindly withdraw the Bill.

provisions were applied. The monetary limit fixed then was Rs.1000/-per 
month which has since been revised to Rs.1500/-per month w.e.f. 9.1.2004. At 
the time of latest amendment to the pr ovision with regard to pension including 
family pension, my Bill on the subject had been introduced which lapsed on the 
completion of my previous term of Membership of the House. It is rather strange 
that nobody took cognizance thereof while amending the provision w.e.f. 
9.1.2004. 
It is a well-established principle relating to family pension that the length 
of the period for which a person whether employee, bureaucrat or a Member of a 
Legislature, has served the State, has to be taken into consideration while 
calculating the pension. Why has this rule not been applied in case of family 
pension , which has also been limited to a fixed period, and that too , at a fixed 
rate , is difficult to be understood? The fallacious position in this regards is 
amply proved by the following two cases. 
1. Sardar Gurcharan singh Tohra died a couple of days before the 
expiring of his term of the Rajya Sabha in  April, 2004 after serving Parliament 
for more than 23 years. A retired Member of Parliament is entiled to a 
minimum pension of Rs. 3000/- per month. For evey year in 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
excess of five years, he is entiled to Rs. 600/- per month. Accordingly, Shri 
Tohra would have been entiled to receive a pension of Rs. 13,800/-per month { 
Rs.3000/- plus Rs. 10,800/-, (that is , Rs.600/- per year for 18 years)} in case of 
retirement in April, 2004, though he had been elected for another term of six years. 
His spouse is now entitled to a pension of Rs. 1500/- per month for a period of 
five years only. In case Shri Tohra would have died after the completion of his 
term and before taking oath for the next term, the spouse would not have been 
entiled to any pension under the existing law. Dr.Abrar Ahmed who died in 
April, 2004, after having served for over eight years, would have been entiled to a 
pension of Rs. 4800/- (Rs.3000/- plus Rs.1800/-) for additional three years in 
excess of five years @ Rs.600/- per y ear) in the event of his having resigned 
from the Membership on the date of his death. His spouse is also entiled to 
have a pension of Rs. 15,00/- that too for a period of five years. 
It is accordingly pertinent, reasonable and logical that the family pension 
provision should take all the relevant aspects such as the length of service 
rendered by the deceased Member etc. into consideration. For the spouse, the 
pension should be for life, and in case of dependents till the dependency lasts 
according to law. The entilement for family pension should be in both the 
cases of death whether it occurs during the tenure of membership or after 
retirement. It is also pertinent to mention that in the cases of both the President and 
Vice-President, the provision for family pension is that the spouse is entiled to fifty 
percent of the pension to which the president / Vice- President would be entiled 
to. 
In the Bill under consideration, suitable provision for family pension have 
been proposed. 
Section 8B about the entilement of conveyance advance is proposed to be 
amended to provide for an advance to a maximum limit of Rs. Four lakh for the 
existing provision of Rs. one lakh (introduced with effect from 26.12.1985 )so 
as to enable a Member seeking this advance to purchase a new vehicle in 
accordance with his status and dignity. 
In the light of submissions made , the Bill may be considered. The 
question was proposed.

amenities and the facilities which are av ailable to the Members of Parliament

Parliament is determined by the Members of Parliament themselves. It is being

to evolve some separate independent mechanism to determine the amenities and 
emoluments of

the Members of Parliament. Because as far as Members of Parliament are 
concerned, we can express our grievanc es, our emergent needs, etc. At the 
same time, we are judging and we are also proclaiming our judgements as far 
as our needs are concerned. So, surely, an unfair mean is there. Therefore, I 
think, some mechanism has to be evolved for determining salaries and 
allowances and providing other amenitie s to the Members of Parliament. This

parliament need to be strengthened. For example, the maximum expenditure is

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I will be very brief since I have Dr. 
M.S. Gill and Shri Rajeev Shukla waiting to speak after me. 
The only reason why I want to speak, Sir, is because this is the only occasion I get to 
express an independent point of view as opposed to the whip that I get from the Chief Whip 
to say the party position. 
Sir, I stand to oppose this Bill because I think this Bill is wrong the way it is 
substantively structured and it is wrong the way it is going to be managed. And I tell you 
why. First and foremost, At a time when the Government is talking about a pension 
crisis—the Central Government spend Rs. 27,000 crores on its pensions and the state 
Governments spends another Rs. 38,000 crores on their pensions—and we are thinking of 
how we can manage the ballooning of the pension crisis, for the lawmakers to enact by 
themselves, for themselves, a pension bonanza, in my view, sends a completely wrong 
signal to the rest of the country. 
On the one hand, we are telling the Government Servants, "Tighten your belts", and 
we are telling the country, "Tighten your belts", on the other, what we are doing is we are 
voting to ourselves a pension increase. And it is not going to stop with pension, because 
today you heard a lot of good ideas on improving the infrastructure, free power, free 
electricity, subsidised housing and so on and so forth. So, it is not going to stop at 
pensions. Pension is only the beginning of the bonanza and, therefore, I oppose this on this 
first ground that at a time when there is a pension payment crisis, at a time when there 
is a serious fiscal crisis for the Central Government and the State Governments, for 
Members of Parliaments to give themselves the right to increase their own allowances 
independently, I think, is wrong and it sends wrong signals. 
Secondly, look at this year's Budget. I wanted to find out how much country spends 
on us. It is quite substantial. It is not a small sum. This year the country would spend 
Rs. 200 crores on 770 Members of Parliament. This Rs. 200 crores is the total amount 
of money that we spend on Malaria Eradication Programme. This Rs. 200 crores is the 
total amount of money that we spend on public health in the entire North-Eastern Region 
which has about 30 million people. So, this is the total am ount of money that the 
Government is already spending only on salaries and allowances. The total expenditure on 
Members of Lok Sabha and 
311 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
Rajya Sabha put together comes to Rs. 300 crores. Out of which, Rs. 200 crores is 
only on salaries and allowances of various kinds. In my view, this is a very substantial 
amount and an increase, at least, doubling the pension, as has been proposed by the hon. 
Member in his Bill, would only add to this crisis. 
Thirdly, a lot of benefits that Members of Parliament get are non-monetised — 
whether it is in terms of housing, whether it is in terms of subsidised communication 
facilities, whether it is in terms of subsidised food that we get in the Central Hall, whether it 
is in terms of subsidised water and electricity. If you really want to move to a clean and 
transparent system, I would agree, you monetise everything and pay the Member of 
Parliament that monetary equivalent and let the Member of Parliament then pay market 
rates for water, market rates for electricity market rate for food, market rate for transport 
and for everything. But, that is not happening. What Members of Parliament and MLAs are 
enjoying today, is not only the benefit allowances but also the benefit of a large number of 
non-monetised allowances like of the type that I have mentioned of which 
predominantly the main benefit is housing. 
What I want to say in brief is this. This is the wrong time to bring about this move. 
It is a wrong way to bring about this move. I quite agree with the suggestion that has 
been made that there must be an independent mechanism in order to evaluate, from 
time to time, what allowances and what benefits that Members of Parliament should get. 
And, I would only end by saying that, today, not only do Members of Parliament enjoy 
pecuniary benefits, but the non-money benefit of being a Member of Parliament is very, 
very substantial. The prestige value associated to being a Member of Parliament can 
never be measures in terms of money value. So, if you look at it from money value 
perspective to say that we are underpaid as compared to the UK or the USA or 
Germany is an unfair comparison. As I mentioned, during my intervention, the Indian 
Parliament works only for 78 days in a year. The UK House of Commons work for 200 
days. The US Congress sits for 210 days in a year. So, if you want to have comparable 
pay-scales, let us also have comparable work standards. Thank you.

Minister will respond to us—is of the security of the passengers in the train. This has
